content: 1. Receiving two doses of the measles vaccine is recommended. Short-term corticosteroid therapy (less than two weeks), topical steroid therapy (e.g., nasal or skin applications), and intra-articular, bursal, or tendon injections with corticosteroids are not considered immunosuppressive and do not contraindicate the administration of the measles vaccine. However, the measles vaccine should be avoided if systemic immunosuppressive levels are reached due to prolonged or extensive topical corticosteroid application. 2. For individuals who cannot receive the measles vaccine but require immediate protection against measles, passive immunization with immune globulin (IG) at a dose of 0.25 mL/kg (0. However, standard doses of IG may not be effective in children with acute leukemia or other conditions associated with altered immunity. For immunocompromised individuals, the recommended IG dose is 0.5 mL/kg of body weight, with a maximum dose of 15 mL. 3. Simultaneous administration of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV), and diphtheria, tetanus toxoids, and pertussis (DTP) vaccines results in seroconversion rates and side effect profiles similar to those observed when the vaccines are administered separately. Based on these findings, the routine simultaneous administration of MMR, OPV, and DTP vaccines is recommended for susceptible individuals at 15 months of age. Some healthcare providers may prefer to administer MMR at 15 months of age, followed by DTP and OPV at 18 months, particularly for patients known to comply with healthcare recommendations. 4. Programs aimed at vaccinating children against measles at 15 months of age should be established and maintained in all communities. Additionally, all other susceptible individuals, regardless of age, should be vaccinated when identified, unless contraindicated. Official health agencies should take necessary steps, including the development and enforcement of school immunization requirements, to achieve and maintain high immunization levels. Most states currently require evidence of measles immunity for children enrolled in daycare centers, and enforcement of such requirements has been associated with reduced measles incidence rates. 5. Measles outbreaks continue to occur in settings where young adults are concentrated, such as colleges. Controlling measles in these environments requires careful evaluation of susceptibility and vaccination of those at risk. It is recommended that colleges and universities require proof of measles immunity as a condition for enrollment. 6. Medical personnel are at a higher risk of acquiring measles compared to the general population. 7. All suspected cases of measles should be investigated promptly. A single confirmed case of measles in a community constitutes an outbreak. Once an outbreak occurs, preventing further spread depends on the rapid vaccination of susceptible individuals. Control activities should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory confirmation of suspected cases. Individuals unable to provide proof of immunity should be vaccinated or excluded from the setting (e.g., school). Documentation of vaccination should include the date of administration. Excluding unvaccinated individuals from outbreak areas has been shown to effectively terminate school outbreaks and increase immunization rates. Students can be readmitted immediately after vaccination. Those exempted from vaccination for medical, religious, or other reasons should be excluded until at least two weeks after the onset of rash in the last measles case in the outbreak area. 8. Persons vaccinated between 12 and 14 months of age may have an increased risk of acquiring measles compared to those vaccinated at 15 months of age, although the increased risk is small. In many outbreaks, particularly in junior and senior high schools, individuals vaccinated at 12–14 months of age have played a significant role in sustaining transmission. Therefore, revaccination of individuals vaccinated at 12–14 months of age should be considered in outbreak settings, especially in high schools. If revaccination is recommended, local officials should define a geographic zone of risk and limit revaccination to individuals within this area. Routine revaccination of individuals vaccinated at 12–14 months of age is not recommended in the absence of an outbreak. 9. Measles importations remain a significant source of reported cases in the United States. While most importations result in limited transmission, some have led to large outbreaks. Rapid reporting of imported cases to state and local health departments is crucial, especially if susceptible individuals were exposed in shared settings like airplanes. 10. As the incidence of measles declines in the United States, aggressive surveillance becomes increasingly important. Known or suspected measles cases should be reported immediately to local health departments. Serologic confirmation should be attempted for all suspected cases that cannot be linked to a confirmed case. Continuous review of adverse events following measles vaccination is also essential. All adverse events should be evaluated and reported in detail to local and state health officials as well as the vaccine manufacturer. 11. Traditional serologic diagnosis of measles requires a significant rise in antibody titers between acute-phase and convalescent-phase serum specimens. However, a single specimen can be used to detect the presence of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies. Proper interpretation of serologic data depends on the timing of specimen collection relative to the onset of symptoms.
